content.text: {"primary_meaning":"The widow most commonly signifies vulnerability, bereavement, social powerlessness, and material need, together with dependence on God and special entitlement to the community’s protection and justice.","primary_basis":["Exodus 22:22–24 — Israel is forbidden to afflict widows, whom God personally defends.","Deuteronomy 10:17–18; 14:28–29; 24:17–22; 27:19 — God executes justice for widows, and Israel must provide for and protect them.","Psalm 68:5; 146:9 — God is the defender and sustainer of widows.","Isaiah 1:17, 23 — care for widows is a test of communal justice and covenant faithfulness.","Jeremiah 7:6–7; 22:3 — oppression of widows exemplifies grave social and covenantal injustice.","James 1:27 — care for widows and orphans epitomizes pure religion.","1 Timothy 5:3–16 — the church is directed to honor and support widows who are truly in need."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Faithful dependence on God, sacrificial generosity, and wholehearted devotion despite poverty.","basis":["1 Kings 17:8–16 — the widow of Zarephath trusts God’s word and gives from scarcity.","Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4 — the poor widow’s offering represents total, costly giving.","Luke 2:36–38 — Anna’s widowhood is associated with sustained worship, fasting, and prayer.","1 Timothy 5:5 — the true widow sets her hope on God and continues in prayer."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Persistence and perseverance in prayer or in seeking justice.","basis":["Luke 18:1–8 — the persistent widow repeatedly petitions an unjust judge; Jesus explicitly applies the parable to continual prayer and confidence in divine justice."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A desolate, abandoned, or conquered city or people, especially Zion/Jerusalem, portrayed as a woman bereft of husband and children.","basis":["Lamentations 1:1 — devastated Jerusalem is described as having become like a widow.","Isaiah 54:4–8 — restored Zion’s former widowhood and abandonment are contrasted with renewed divine compassion.","Revelation 18:7 — Babylon’s boast that she is not a widow anticipates her sudden desolation and judgment."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The Church, Israel, or the individual soul temporarily bereft of the visible presence of the divine Bridegroom and therefore longing for reunion with him.","basis":["Matthew 9:15; Mark 2:19–20; Luke 5:34–35 — the Bridegroom’s removal provides the broader imagery behind later Christian allegory.","Isaiah 54:4–8 and Lamentations 1:1 — Zion’s widowhood supplied language for ecclesial and spiritual applications.","Luke 2:36–38; 1 Timothy 5:5 — devout widowhood was sometimes applied typologically to prayerful waiting for God."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Corrupt or falsely secure religious or imperial power claiming independence and immunity from loss.","basis":["Revelation 18:7 — Babylon declares, “I sit as a queen; I am no widow,” before judgment.","Isaiah 47:7–9 — Babylon’s confidence is overturned by widowhood and loss of children."],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is no single settled symbolic definition of “widow” across Christian interpretation. Most biblical uses are literal, and the broadest recurring theological motif is the widow as the paradigmatic vulnerable person whom God defends and God’s people must protect. Other meanings arise from particular narratives, parables, prophetic personifications, and later allegorical interpretation."}
